newsitem.title: USA: Catholic Archbishop opposes death for McVeigh.
newsitem.headline: Catholic Archbishop opposes death for McVeigh.

text.p: The Catholic Archbishop of Denver, voicing concern at what he called a "vengeful" spirit in society, said on Tuesday that he hoped convicted Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh would not be sentenced to death.

Archbishop Charles Chaput spoke with reporters about the Catholic Church's position on the death penalty, as a jury in Denver weighed whether McVeigh should be sentenced to death or life imprisonment for the April 19, 1995 bombing of the Alfred P. Murrah federal building that killed 168 people.

Chaput said the jury in the McVeigh case was in a very difficult position. "I pray that they make a decision that serves society in the long run -- and that decision, from my perspective, is to give the man life imprisonment and not execution," he said.
Prosecutors are pushing for the death penalty for McVeigh, 29, convicted last week of the worst mass murder in U.S. history. The defence is seeking life imprisonment.
Chaput said the Catholic Church opposed the death penalty except in exceptional circumstances where it was the only way for society to defend itself.

The Catholic Church believes that "in contemporary Western society it is almost never the case that we need to execute criminals, even very guilty, evil criminals, in order to protect society from them," he said.

The only situation he could think of where execution might be applicable would be "a criminal who kills other criminals in jails or is a danger to guards ... A state theoretically has a right to defend itself."

Chaput said McVeigh needed to be punished severely but that executing him would not take away the pain of the families of the bombing victims. "It doesn't do anything for anyone except bring more violence into the world," he said.
"Violence isn't a solution to life's problems," he said. "The only real solution to violence in our lives ... is to find some way of forgiving."

Refering to the McVeigh case, Chaput said he was disturbed by some of the "violent kind of vengeful reactions that I see in society." "There is a tremendous kind of popular violence in the response of some of the people in our community," he said, stressing that he was not refering to the relatives of bombing victims whose anger, he said, was understandable.
"We've become a country that executes people one after the other. What are we teaching our young people about violence as a solution to life's problems?" Chaput asked.
